topics.name: Data and sampling
topics.line: Statistics is <mark>using data to make a decision</mark>. You rarely get to check everyone, so you check a slice (a sample) and use it to say something about the whole group (the population).

ex.text: You want the first-serve percentage of every player on tour this season (the population). You can't chart every match, so you chart 200 (the sample). The sample number is p hat; the true number is p.

qa: Describe means summarize what you have. Infer means use a sample to say something about the bigger group.
A team's average age is describing. A poll predicting an election is inferring.
A gym surveys 150 of its 2,400 members. Population and sample?
Population: all 2,400 members. Sample: the 150 surveyed.
Random is fair to everyone, stratified makes every group show up, risk-based oversamples the riskiest group.
An auditor checking expense reports looks hardest at the largest claims.
300 expense reports out of 50,000: how do you pick?
Stratify by amount, oversample the largest claims, pick at random inside each group, then reweight to the real shares when you add it up.
All 300 from small claims tells you nothing about the big ones, where the money is.
No, qualitative. An average zip code means nothing.
Price, square feet, and bedrooms for each home?
topics.trap: A bigger sample fixes randomness but not bias. 10,000 app users who answered a survey still tell you nothing about the users who ignore surveys. That is a convenience sample.
topics.hook: A name is a label, a price is a number. Everyone on tour is the population; the 200 matches you charted are the sample.
links: Chapter 1, about 10 minutes. Sampling is the first idea.
Search sampling methods and do 5 practice questions.
formulas: Quantitative: numbers you can average. Qualitative: labels.
Population: N, μ, σ, p. Sample: n, x̄, s, p̂.

topics.name: Where is the middle
topics.line: Mean is the average. Median is the middle once sorted. Mode is the most common. The big idea: one extreme number drags the mean, and the median barely moves.

ex.text: Ranking points for the top 100: a few players hold huge totals, so the mean sits way above the median. Ask what a typical top-100 player has and you want the median.

qa: Sorted: 0 5 7 7 11 15 22 29. Average the middle two, 7 and 11.
A few mansions blow up the mean.
The tail pulls the mean toward it.
To stop outliers pulling the average. Drop the top and bottom 5%, average the rest.
Useful when tails are heavy, like incomes or claim sizes.
Fund A averages 6% a year, fund B averages 14%. Which is better?
Can't say yet. You need the risk.
The average alone hides how bumpy the ride is. That is the next topic.
topics.trap: Duplicates count. In 15, 7, 22, 7, 29, 11, 5, 0 the 7 appears twice, and both copies stay in the sorted list.
topics.hook: Mean is the average salary with the boss in the room. Median is what the typical person makes. The mean chases the tail.
links: Search the channel for mean median mode.
Skip for now; come back for topic 4.
formulas: x̄ = Σx / n for a sample, μ = Σx / N for a population
Sort, take the middle; average the two middles if n is even
Most frequent value; none if all differ, bimodal if two tie
Right skew: mode < median < mean. Left skew: mean < median < mode.

topics.name: How spread out is it
topics.line: Range is the biggest value minus the smallest. Standard deviation is how far a typical value sits from the average. In finance SD is risk. The empirical rule: 68% within 1 SD, 95% within 2, almost all within 3, when the data is hill shaped.

ex.text: Your first serve averages 115 mph with an SD of 5. About two thirds of serves land between 110 and 120, and 95% between 105 and 125. A 132 mph serve is more than 3 SD out; either the radar gun glitched or something changed.

qa: 75 minus 12. One extreme value sets the whole range.
One outlier sets it, it ignores the middle, and it grows with n.
Why square the gaps from the mean?
A sample hugs its own average and looks too tight; one less pushes the variance back up.
4, 7, 10: 18 ÷ 2 = 9 as a sample vs 18 ÷ 3 = 6 as a population.
No. Zero only if every value is identical.
Mean 400, SD 50: where do 95% of days land?
What share of days sell more than 450?
32% sit outside 1 SD, half of them on top.
When does the empirical rule fail?
Skewed, bimodal, or outlier-heavy data. Market returns have fat tails.
So consistent that only about 3 in a million come out bad.
The limit sits 6 SD from the average.
topics.trap: Same range, different spread. 10, 50, 50, 50, 90 and 10, 10, 50, 90, 90 both have a range of 80, yet their standard deviations are about 28 and 40. Range only sees the two ends; standard deviation sees every value.
topics.hook: Most Days Start Slow, Dude, Relax: mean, distance, square, sum, divide, root. SD is how bumpy the ride is. 1 SD happens most days, 2 SD about once a month, 3 SD about once a year.
links: Search the channel for standard deviation clearly explained.
Art of Stat: Explore Quantitative Data
Paste 4, 7, 10 and read the SD, then add 40 and watch it jump.
formulas: x̄ ± 1s holds 68%, x̄ ± 2s holds 95%, x̄ ± 3s holds 99.7%

topics.name: Probability rules
topics.line: List everything that can happen. Or means add and subtract the overlap. And means multiply. Given means shrink the list to what you were told and count inside it. Mutually exclusive means both can't happen; independent means one tells you nothing about the other.

ex.text: Break-point conversion is a conditional probability: P(win the point | it is a break point). You only count the break points, and that is the given. A player converts 20 of 50, so 40%.

qa: Two coins and a die: how many outcomes?
One die roll: P(not a 1 or 2)?
A = {1, 2, 3}, B = {3, 4} on one die roll. P(A or B)?
From a pack of 52 cards: P(heart or face card)?
13 + 12 − 3. Don't count the heart face cards twice.
Die roll: P(5 or 6 given the roll is above 2)?
The list shrinks to 3, 4, 5, 6, and two of those count.
60% of hotel guests use the gym, 30% use the spa, 12% use both. P(spa given gym)?
Two aces in a row, no replacement?
One ace and one card are gone.
Flight on time 0.85, bag arrives given on time 0.95: both?
Bag arrives given late is 0.70. Your bag arrived. Chance the flight was on time?
Add the two bag-arrives branches for 0.9125, then shrink.
topics.trap: Mutually exclusive events are not independent. If A happens B cannot, so knowing A changes B completely.
topics.hook: Or is two guest lists (count people on both once). And is a combo lock (every dial has to hit, so multiply). Given is a filter (narrow the list, then count). Mutually exclusive is a coin landing heads and tails at once.
links: Set theory, conditional probability, Bayes. About 15 minutes.
Search conditional probability and do the practice set.
formulas: 0 ≤ P(A) ≤ 1, all outcomes add to 1, P(not A) = 1 − P(A)
P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B)
P(A | B) = P(A and B) / P(B)
P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B | A); if independent, P(A) × P(B)
Multiply along a branch, add branches with the same ending

topics.name: Random variables and expected value
topics.line: A <mark>random variable</mark> is a number whose value depends on chance. Its <mark>expected value</mark> is the probability-weighted average: what you'd get on average over many repeats. Its <mark>SD</mark> is the risk around that average.

ex.text: Investment A returns 2% or 14% with equal odds: E = 8%, σ = 6%. Investment B returns −6, 6, 12, 24 with odds 0.1, 0.3, 0.4, 0.2: E = 10.8%, σ = 8.4%. B pays more, but A has the lower CV (75% vs 78%), so A wins on return per unit of risk.

qa: Expected value of one roll of a four-sided die (1 to 4)?
Weighted average. You never roll a 2.5; it is the long-run average.
Toss 3 coins, Y = number of heads. E(Y)?
Shifting every outcome shifts the mean, not the spread.
A or B on expected value? On risk? On both?
topics.trap: The expected value is not the most likely outcome and may be impossible to observe (2.5 on a four-sided die). It is the long-run average.
topics.hook: Expected value is what a bet is worth on average if you took it a thousand times. SD is how far a single try can land from that. CV is risk per unit of reward: lower is better.
links: Expectation and variance you can drag and watch. About 10 minutes.
Search the channel for expected values.
formulas: σ² = Σ (y − μ)² · P(y) = Σ y²P(y) − μ²
E(a + bY) = a + b · E(Y), Var(a + bY) = b² · Var(Y)

topics.name: Two variables: covariance, correlation, portfolios
topics.line: Covariance asks whether two things move together. Correlation is covariance scaled to run from −1 to +1. Put two assets together and any correlation below +1 lowers the risk of the mix. That is diversification.

ex.text: Asset A: E = 8%, σ = 6%. Asset B: E = 10.8%, σ = 8.4%. Covariance 12.6, so ρ = 12.6 / (6 × 8.4) = 0.25. A 50/50 mix returns 9.4% with σ = 5.74%, lower than either asset alone.

qa: They tend to move in the same direction
Not necessarily. Y = X² can have zero covariance and total dependence.
Zero covariance rules out only a straight-line relationship.
50/50 mix of A and B: expected return?
Why is the mix less risky than both assets?
ρ is only 0.25; the cross term is small and the squared weights shrink the rest.
topics.trap: Independent implies Cov = 0, but Cov = 0 does not imply independent. Y = X² is the classic example built to catch this.
topics.hook: Correlation is why you don't put all your eggs in one basket. The last term in the variance formula is the only place the two assets talk to each other.
links: Drag the correlation control and watch the scatter. About 5 minutes.
formulas: Cov(X, Y) = ΣΣ (x − μx)(y − μy) P(x, y) = ΣΣ xy P(x, y) − μx μy
ρ = Cov(X, Y) / (σx σy), between −1 and 1
E(bX + cY) = b · E(X) + c · E(Y)
V(bX + cY) = b²V(X) + c²V(Y) + 2bc · Cov(X, Y)

topics.name: Counting and the binomial
topics.line: When you repeat a yes-or-no trial n times with the same chance p each time, the number of yeses is <mark>binomial</mark>. The mean is np and the variance is np(1 − p). Counting rules (factorials, combinations) tell you how many ways the yeses can be arranged.

ex.text: You win 60% of tiebreaks. In a five-set match with 3 tiebreaks, P(win exactly 2) = C(3,2)(0.6)²(0.4) = 43.2%. P(win at least 1) = 1 − 0.4³ = 93.6%.

qa: Gold and silver from 5 runners: how many orders?
Pick 2 of 5 runners for a pair, order doesn't matter?
Fixed n, two outcomes, independent trials, the same p every time
20% of shoppers use a coupon, n = 8: P(exactly 2)?
A free throw goes in 70% of the time. 4 shots: P(exactly 3)?
topics.trap: At least one is 1 − P(none). Adding P(1) + P(2) + … by hand wastes time and invites arithmetic errors.
topics.hook: Binomial is counting wins in a fixed number of matches when every match is the same weighted coin.
links: Pick Binomial, drag n and p. About 8 minutes.
formulas: BINOM.DIST(y, n, p, FALSE) for exactly y; TRUE for at most y

topics.name: Poisson: counts per unit
topics.line: Poisson counts how many events land in a fixed window (a minute, an hour, a page) when they arrive at a steady average rate λ. The mean and the variance are both λ. Scale λ to the window first.

ex.text: You hit 3 unforced errors per set on average. P(zero in a set) = e⁻³ = 5%. Over a 3-set match λ = 9, so P(at most 6) is about 21%.

qa: A coffee shop gets 30 orders per hour. λ for 10 minutes?
Scale the rate to the window.
P(2 or more orders in 10 minutes)?
With one barista, a second order means someone waits.
A help desk gets 3 calls per hour. P(exactly 3 in one hour)?
P(4 or fewer calls in 2 hours)?
topics.trap: Forgetting to rescale λ. 3 calls per hour over 2 hours is λ = 6, not 3.
topics.hook: Poisson is for counting arrivals: calls to a help desk, emails in an hour, errors per set. Pick the time window first, then count.
links: Pick Poisson, drag λ. About 5 minutes.
formulas: λ for a window = rate × window length
POISSON.DIST(y, λ, FALSE) for exactly y; TRUE for at most y

topics.name: The normal curve and z
topics.line: The <mark>normal</mark> is the bell. Any normal becomes the standard one by measuring in SDs from the mean: <mark>z = (y − μ) / σ</mark>. Then a z table (or NORM.S.DIST) gives the area, and area is probability.

ex.text: A cafe sells 400 coffees a day on average, with an SD of 50. P(more than 475) is z = 1.5, and the area above is 6.7%. Stock 464 cups and you run out on about 10% of days (z = 1.28).

qa: How many cups so P(running out) ≤ 0.10?
What does a z of −2 mean?
1, half on each side of the mean
Delivery times ~ N(32, 6) minutes: P(more than 35)?
topics.trap: Some z tables give the area from 0 to z, not from the far left. Add 0.5 for less than a positive z. Excel's NORM.S.DIST gives the cumulative area from the left.
topics.hook: z is how many SDs away from average. 1.28, 1.645, 1.96, 2.576: memorize those four and every bell-curve question becomes arithmetic.
links: Pick Normal, drag μ and σ. About 8 minutes.
Type μ, σ, and a cutoff; it shades the area.
Search the channel for normal distribution clearly explained.
formulas: z = (y − μ) / σ, and back again y = μ + zσ
P(Y < y) = Φ(z), P(Y > y) = 1 − Φ(z), P(a < Y < b) = Φ(z_b) − Φ(z_a)
NORM.DIST(y, μ, σ, TRUE), NORM.S.DIST(z, TRUE), NORM.INV(p, μ, σ)

topics.name: Sampling distributions and the CLT
topics.line: Take a sample and compute its mean. Take another and compute again. Those sample means have their own distribution, and the <mark>Central Limit Theorem</mark> says it is close to normal once n is big enough, centered on μ with spread <mark>σ / √n</mark> (the standard error). The same works for proportions.

ex.text: One match's first-serve percentage bounces around. Average 36 matches and the noise shrinks by √36 = 6. A player at 62% with a match-to-match SD of 6 points has a 36-match average with a standard error of 1 point, so it almost always lands within 2 points of 62.

qa: Why can we use the normal there?
n is above 30, so the CLT applies even if the population isn't normal
Repair bills: mean 640, SD 480, n = 64. SE?
The total has mean 40,960 and SD 480√64 = 3,840; z = 0.792.
It depends on skew. Textbooks say 30. A normal population works at any n.
Is a statistic a random variable?
Yes. It changes from sample to sample.
topics.trap: Dividing σ by n instead of √n. The standard error shrinks with the square root, so quadrupling the sample only halves the noise.
topics.hook: Averaging is noise cancelling. The √n is the price: four times the data only buys half the noise.
links: Point estimation and the CLT animation. About 10 minutes; watch it twice.
Search the channel for central limit theorem.
formulas: Centered on μ with standard error σ / √n
Mean p, SE = √[p(1 − p) / n], normal if np ≥ 10 and n(1 − p) ≥ 10
Close to normal for large n (rule of thumb 30), whatever the population looks like

topics.name: Confidence intervals and sample size
topics.line: A point estimate is one number. A <mark>confidence interval</mark> is that number plus and minus a margin: <mark>estimate ± critical value × standard error</mark>. Use z when σ is known and t when you only have s. Flip the formula around and it tells you how big a sample you need.

ex.text: You charted 20 matches: average first-serve speed 115 mph, s = 6. 95% CI: 115 ± 2.093 × 6/√20 = 115 ± 2.8, so 112.2 to 117.8. Want ±1 mph at 95%? n = (1.96 × 6 / 1)² ≈ 139 matches.

qa: 25 bottles, x̄ = 502.4 ml, σ = 5 known: 95% CI?
σ is unknown, so you used s. Fatter tails, bigger multiplier.
t gets close to z as n grows.
120 of 200 prefer the new app: 90% CI for p?
Proportion, interval width 0.06 at 95%, no prior guess: n?
Same, but p is known to sit between 0.10 and 0.20?
Use 0.20; it gives the larger n.
95% of intervals built this way contain μ. Any one interval either does or doesn't.
topics.trap: A 95% CI is not a 95% chance that μ is in here. μ is fixed; the interval is what moves. Also, for sample size the width is 2E, so a width of 0.06 means E = 0.03.
topics.hook: A confidence interval is a margin of error around your guess. More confidence widens it, more data tightens it, and σ is the part you can't control.
links: Confidence interval section: watch intervals miss μ. About 8 minutes.
Art of Stat: Inference for a Mean
formulas: n = z² p(1 − p) / E², using p = 0.5 with no prior estimate

topics.name: Simple regression
topics.line: <mark>Regression</mark> fits the straight line that makes the squared vertical misses as small as possible. The <mark>slope</mark> says how much y moves per unit of x. <mark>R²</mark> says what share of y's variation the line explains. The <mark>t-test on the slope</mark> asks whether x helps at all.

ex.text: Does advertising move sales? Six weeks of data give Sales = 1.43 + 1.14 Adv: each extra unit of advertising adds about 1.14 units of sales. R² = 87.1% means the line explains most of the scatter, and t = 5.19 (p = 0.007) says that isn't luck.

qa: Σx = 24, Σy = 36, Σxy = 176, Σx² = 124, n = 6. Slope?
Predict sales at 8 units of advertising?
87.1% of the variation in sales is explained by advertising
About 95% of prediction errors are within ± 2.32
The CI is for the average y at x; the PI is for one new y, so it is wider
Mean zero, constant variance, normal, independent
An x far from the other x values. It can swing the line.
A common flag is leverage above 6/n.
topics.trap: Correlation is symmetric; regression is not. Swapping x and y gives a different line. And never predict outside the range of x you have.
topics.hook: Slope is rise over run. R² is how much of the scatter the line explains. The t-test asks whether the slope is really different from zero or just noise.
links: Drag points and watch the least squares line chase them. About 10 minutes.
Search the channel for linear regression clearly explained. Worth watching before you start regression.
formulas: SST = SSR + SSE, R² = SSR / SST = 1 − SSE / SST
r = ±√R², with the sign of the slope

topics.name: Multiple regression
topics.line: The same idea with several x's: fit a plane instead of a line. Each coefficient is the effect of its x <mark>holding the others fixed</mark>. The <mark>F-test</mark> asks if the model as a whole helps; each <mark>t-test</mark> asks if one x adds anything given the rest. <mark>Multicollinearity</mark> is when two x's say the same thing.

ex.text: Home prices on square feet and number of rooms: each predicts price on its own, but together the rooms coefficient can flip negative and stop being significant, because bigger homes have more rooms. With a correlation of 0.95 between them, VIF = 1 / (1 − 0.95²) ≈ 10.3, and the model can't tell which one is doing the work.

qa: Price = 42 + 0.118 SqFt + 6.5 Garage, price in $1,000s. Interpret 0.118.
Each extra square foot adds about $118 to the price, holding garage spaces fixed
Only valid inside the range of homes in the data.
Reject H₀. At least one x has predictive value.
Square footage adds predictive value to a model that already has garage spaces
Adjusted R² penalizes extra predictors; it is never above R²
That x is highly correlated with the other x's. Multicollinearity.
Wrong signs, big coefficient swings when a variable is added, a significant x going insignificant, s going up
One dummy: 1 for a corner lot, 0 otherwise
Sequential SS: SqFt first gives 52.0, Garage adds 8.0. Garage first gives 38.5. What does SqFt add?
Order changes the split, not the total.
topics.trap: Holding other variables fixed is a statement about the math, not the world. If square footage and rooms move together in reality, you can't hold one fixed.
topics.hook: Multiple regression is a recipe with several ingredients. F asks if the recipe works at all. Each t asks if one ingredient earns its place. VIF is the alarm for two ingredients that are the same thing.
links: Search the channel for multiple regression clearly explained.
Search least squares regression and do the practice set.
formulas: F = MSR / MSE, df (k, n − k − 1)
t = bⱼ / SE(bⱼ), df = n − k − 1
k categories need k − 1 indicator columns

fw.intro: Five tools that work on any business statistics problem. Use the first one on an exam when you freeze: answer three questions and it hands you the formula.
fw.loop: This is spaced retrieval practice with interleaving, the two study techniques with the strongest evidence (Dunlosky et al., 2013). Ten minutes a day through the loop beats an hour of rereading. The draw on Practice only fills in from drills, on purpose.

copy.heroSub: Thirteen topics, each with one plain sentence, a real example, and questions with the answers highlighted. Nine come with a lab to drag. Then drill with fresh numbers until it sticks.
copy.drillIntro: Fresh numbers every time, a clock, and a score. The timed closed-book mock is 20 mixed questions, calculator only.
copy.mockSaved: Mock score saved as exam readiness.
copy.sheetIntro: Print this. Every formula, when to use it, and a worked example, with answers highlighted.
